P1● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

The prime factorisation of 588 is:

repeated division; every factor must be prime and the product must be 588 (Topic 2). Why it applies: each option must pass both tests.

All factors prime; 4×3×49=5884 \times 3 \times 49 = 5884×3×49=588.
The value is right, but 4 and 49 are composite — not a prime factorisation.
6 is composite.
All factors are prime, but 4×9×7=2524 \times 9 \times 7 = 2524×9×7=252, not 588 — a miscount of the 3s and 7s.

Given: 588. Asked: its prime factorisation.

Concept used: repeated division; every factor must be prime and the product must be 588 (Topic 2). Why it applies: each option must pass both tests.

  1. 1

    588÷2=294588 \div 2 = 294588÷2=294, 294÷2=147294 \div 2 = 147294÷2=147, 147÷3=49147 \div 3 = 49147÷3=49, 49÷7=749 \div 7 = 749÷7=7, 7÷7=17 \div 7 = 17÷7=1.

  2. 2

    So 588=22×3×72588 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7^2588=22×3×72.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✔ All factors prime; 4×3×49=5884 \times 3 \times 49 = 5884×3×49=588.
    • (b) ✘ The value is right, but 4 and 49 are composite — not a prime factorisation.
    • (c) ✘ 6 is composite.
    • (d) ✘ All factors are prime, but 4×9×7=2524 \times 9 \times 7 = 2524×9×7=252, not 588 — a miscount of the 3s and 7s.

  3. Check: 22×3×72=4×147=5882^2 \times 3 \times 7^2 = 4 \times 147 = 58822×3×72=4×147=588 ✔.

  4. Answer (a)

    Common trap: Choosing (b) because "the product is correct". A prime factorisation needs prime factors and the right product.
P2● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

Express 2 772 as a product of its prime factors.

Full solution

Given: 2 772. Asked: its prime factorisation.

Concept used: repeated division (Topic 2). Why it applies: 2 772 is even and its digit sum is 18.

  1. 1

    Divide by 2.

    2772÷2=13862772 \div 2 = 13862772÷2=1386Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Divide by 2.

    1386÷2=6931386 \div 2 = 6931386÷2=693Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Digit sum of 693 is 18: divide by 3.

    693÷3=231693 \div 3 = 231693÷3=231Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Digit sum of 231 is 6: divide by 3.

    231÷3=77231 \div 3 = 77231÷3=77Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    77=7×1177 = 7 \times 1177=7×11.

    2772=22×32×7×112772 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7 \times 112772=22×32×7×11Swipe to see the whole equation →

  6. Check: 4×9=364 \times 9 = 364×9=36, 36×77=277236 \times 77 = 277236×77=2772 ✔.

  7. Answer 2772=22×32×7×112772 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7 \times 112772=22×32×7×11

    Common trap: Stopping at 693 or 231 — both are composite (digit sums divisible by 3).

P3● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

The HCF of 23×52×112^3 \times 5^2 \times 1123×52×11 and 24×5×72^4 \times 5 \times 724×5×7 is:

HCF = smallest power of each common prime (Topic 3). Why it applies: the numbers are already factorised.

Smallest powers of the common primes.
Largest powers of the common primes — the min/max swap.
This is the LCM.
7 and 11 are not common, so they cannot be in the HCF.

Given: two factorisations. Asked: their HCF.

Concept used: HCF = smallest power of each common prime (Topic 3). Why it applies: the numbers are already factorised.

  1. 1

    Common primes: 2 and 5 (7 and 11 are each in only one number).

  2. 2

    Smallest powers: 232^323 and 515^151.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✔ Smallest powers of the common primes.
    • (b) ✘ Largest powers of the common primes — the min/max swap.
    • (c) ✘ This is the LCM.
    • (d) ✘ 7 and 11 are not common, so they cannot be in the HCF.

  3. Check: 23×5=402^3 \times 5 = 4023×5=40; 404040 divides 220022002200 and 560560560 ✔.

  4. Answer (a)

P4● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Find the HCF and LCM of 90 and 132 by the prime factorisation method, and verify that HCF × LCM = product of the numbers.

Full solution

Given: 90 and 132. Asked: HCF, LCM and the verification.

Concept used: prime-power table; HCF × LCM = product for two numbers (Topic 3). Why it applies: exactly two numbers.

  1. 1

    Factorise.

    90=2×32×5,132=22×3×1190 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5, \qquad 132 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 1190=2×32×5,132=22×3×11Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    HCF: common primes 2 and 3, smallest powers.

    HCF=2×3=6\text{HCF} = 2 \times 3 = 6HCF=2×3=6Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    LCM: largest powers of 2, 3, 5, 11.

    LCM=22×32×5×11=1980\text{LCM} = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 11 = 1980LCM=22×32×5×11=1980Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Verify.

    6×1980=11 880,90×132=11 8806 \times 1980 = 11\,880, \qquad 90 \times 132 = 11\,8806×1980=11880,90×132=11880Swipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: 1980÷90=221980 \div 90 = 221980÷90=22, 1980÷132=151980 \div 132 = 151980÷132=15 ✔.

  6. Answer HCF=6,LCM=1980\text{HCF} = 6, \quad \text{LCM} = 1980HCF=6,LCM=1980; 6×1980=11 880=90×1326 \times 1980 = 11\,880 = 90 \times 1326×1980=11880=90×132 ✔

    Common trap: Writing 132=2×66132 = 2 \times 66132=2×66 and using 66 as a "prime". Every factor must be prime: 132=22×3×11132 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 11132=22×3×11.

P5● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which of these situations needs the HCF?

cutting or measuring into the largest equal parts → HCF; waiting for cycles to line up, or the smallest common multiple → LCM (Topic 4). Why it applies: decide what is really happening in each.

Waiting for two cycles to line up → LCM (60 s).
The number must be a multiple of both 12 and 15, as small as possible → LCM (60).
The rod length must divide both 360 and 450, as long as possible → HCF (90 cm).
Meeting at the start → LCM (12 min).

Given: four situations. Asked: which needs the HCF.

Concept used: cutting or measuring into the largest equal parts → HCF; waiting for cycles to line up, or the smallest common multiple → LCM (Topic 4). Why it applies: decide what is really happening in each.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Waiting for two cycles to line up → LCM (60 s).
    • (b) ✘ The number must be a multiple of both 12 and 15, as small as possible → LCM (60).
    • (c) ✔ The rod length must divide both 360 and 450, as long as possible → HCF (90 cm).
    • (d) ✘ Meeting at the start → LCM (12 min).

  2. Check: 360=90×4360 = 90 \times 4360=90×4, 450=90×5450 = 90 \times 5450=90×5 ✔.

  3. Answer (c)

    Common trap: Picking (b) because it says "shared equally". The sweets are a common multiple of 12 and 15; it is the group size that would be a factor.
P6● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

For which of these can the number end with the digit 0 for some natural number n?

ending in 0 needs both 2 and 5 in the prime factorisation; knk^nkn has the same primes as k (Topic 2). Why it applies: factorise each base.

8n=23n8^n = 2^{3n}8n=23n — a 2 but no 5.
15n=3n×5n15^n = 3^n \times 5^n15n=3n×5n — a 5 but no 2.
21n=3n×7n21^n = 3^n \times 7^n21n=3n×7n — neither 2 nor 5.
30n=2n×3n×5n30^n = 2^n \times 3^n \times 5^n30n=2n×3n×5n — both 2 and 5, so it ends in 0 for every n.

Given: four powers. Asked: which can end in 0.

Concept used: ending in 0 needs both 2 and 5 in the prime factorisation; knk^nkn has the same primes as k (Topic 2). Why it applies: factorise each base.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ 8n=23n8^n = 2^{3n}8n=23n — a 2 but no 5.
    • (b) ✘ 15n=3n×5n15^n = 3^n \times 5^n15n=3n×5n — a 5 but no 2.
    • (c) ✘ 21n=3n×7n21^n = 3^n \times 7^n21n=3n×7n — neither 2 nor 5.
    • (d) ✔ 30n=2n×3n×5n30^n = 2^n \times 3^n \times 5^n30n=2n×3n×5n — both 2 and 5, so it ends in 0 for every n.

  2. Check: 302=90030^2 = 900302=900 ✔.

  3. Answer (d)

P7● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which of these numbers is irrational?

rational = pq\dfrac{p}{q}qp​ (decimal terminates or repeats); the root of a non-square whole number is irrational (Topics 1 and 5). Why it applies: test each option.

196=14\sqrt{196} = 14196​=14, rational.
0.4444…=490.4444\ldots = \dfrac{4}{9}0.4444…=94​, a repeating decimal, rational.
50 is not a perfect square: 50=52\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}50​=52​, irrational.
227\dfrac{22}{7}722​ is a fraction of integers — rational (it only approximates π\piπ).

Given: four numbers. Asked: the irrational one.

Concept used: rational = pq\dfrac{p}{q}qp​ (decimal terminates or repeats); the root of a non-square whole number is irrational (Topics 1 and 5). Why it applies: test each option.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ 196=14\sqrt{196} = 14196​=14, rational.
    • (b) ✘ 0.4444…=490.4444\ldots = \dfrac{4}{9}0.4444…=94​, a repeating decimal, rational.
    • (c) ✔ 50 is not a perfect square: 50=52\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}50​=52​, irrational.
    • (d) ✘ 227\dfrac{22}{7}722​ is a fraction of integers — rational (it only approximates π\piπ).

  2. Check: 72=49<50<64=827^2 = 49 < 50 < 64 = 8^272=49<50<64=82, so 50 is not a perfect square ✔.

  3. Answer (c)

P8● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

The HCF of 6, 10 and 15 is 1 and their LCM is 30. The product 6×10×156 \times 10 \times 156×10×15 is:

multiply directly — HCF × LCM = product holds for two numbers only (Topic 3). Why it applies: there are three numbers.

Uses the two-number rule for three numbers.
6×10×15=9006 \times 10 \times 15 = 9006×10×15=900.
Adds the HCF and LCM.
Multiplies the LCM by 6 only.

Given: HCF = 1, LCM = 30 for 6, 10, 15. Asked: the product of the three numbers.

Concept used: multiply directly — HCF × LCM = product holds for two numbers only (Topic 3). Why it applies: there are three numbers.

  1. 1

    Multiply.

    6×10×15=9006 \times 10 \times 15 = 9006×10×15=900Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Compare: HCF × LCM =1×30=30= 1 \times 30 = 30=1×30=30, which is not 900.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Uses the two-number rule for three numbers.
    • (b) ✔ 6×10×15=9006 \times 10 \times 15 = 9006×10×15=900.
    • (c) ✘ Adds the HCF and LCM.
    • (d) ✘ Multiplies the LCM by 6 only.

  3. Check: 60×15=90060 \times 15 = 90060×15=900 ✔.

  4. Answer (b)

    Common trap: Answer (a) — the most common error with three numbers. The product rule is for two numbers only.
P9● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

In a proof that 7\sqrt{7}7​ is irrational, we assume 7=ab\sqrt{7} = \dfrac{a}{b}7​=ba​. Which condition must we state about a and b?

the seven-stage template (Topic 5). Why it applies: the contradiction at the end ("7 divides both a and b") only works if a and b were co-prime.

Integers (so ab\dfrac{a}{b}ba​ is rational), b≠0b \neq 0b=0 (a fraction needs a non-zero denominator), co-prime (any fraction can be reduced — and this is what the contradiction breaks).
There is no reason to assume this.
True (7>1\sqrt{7} > 17​>1) but irrelevant to the contradiction.
That would mean 7\sqrt{7}7​ is a whole number — not what we assume.

Given: the first line of the proof. Asked: the condition on a and b.

Concept used: the seven-stage template (Topic 5). Why it applies: the contradiction at the end ("7 divides both a and b") only works if a and b were co-prime.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✔ Integers (so ab\dfrac{a}{b}ba​ is rational), b≠0b \neq 0b=0 (a fraction needs a non-zero denominator), co-prime (any fraction can be reduced — and this is what the contradiction breaks).
    • (b) ✘ There is no reason to assume this.
    • (c) ✘ True (7>1\sqrt{7} > 17​>1) but irrelevant to the contradiction.
    • (d) ✘ That would mean 7\sqrt{7}7​ is a whole number — not what we assume.

  2. Check: without "co-prime", step 6 ("7 divides a and b") contradicts nothing ✔.

  3. Answer (a)

P10●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Find the HCF and LCM of 84, 126 and 210. Show that the product of the three numbers is not equal to HCF × LCM.

Full solution

Given: 84, 126, 210. Asked: HCF, LCM, and the comparison.

Concept used: prime-power table for three numbers (Topic 3). Why it applies: with three numbers, we must not use the product rule.

  1. 1

    Factorise.

    84=22×3×7,126=2×32×7,210=2×3×5×784 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7, \qquad 126 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 7, \qquad 210 = 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 784=22×3×7,126=2×32×7,210=2×3×5×7Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    HCF: primes in all three are 2, 3, 7; smallest powers.

    HCF=2×3×7=42\text{HCF} = 2 \times 3 \times 7 = 42HCF=2×3×7=42Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    LCM: largest powers 222^222, 323^232, 5, 7.

    LCM=22×32×5×7=1260\text{LCM} = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 1260LCM=22×32×5×7=1260Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    HCF × LCM.

    42×1260=52 92042 \times 1260 = 52\,92042×1260=52920Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Product of the numbers.

    84×126×210=2 222 64084 \times 126 \times 210 = 2\,222\,64084×126×210=2222640Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    52 920≠2 222 64052\,920 \neq 2\,222\,64052920=2222640 (the product is 42 times bigger).

  7. Check: 1260÷84=151260 \div 84 = 151260÷84=15, 1260÷126=101260 \div 126 = 101260÷126=10, 1260÷210=61260 \div 210 = 61260÷210=6 ✔.

  8. Answer HCF = 424242, LCM = 126012601260; HCF × LCM = 52 920 ≠ 2 222 640 = 84×126×21084 \times 126 \times 21084×126×210.

    Common trap: Finding the LCM as 84×126×21042=52 920\dfrac{84 \times 126 \times 210}{42} = 52\,9204284×126×210​=52920 — 42 times too big.

P14●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

A gardener has 360 rose plants and 540 marigold plants. She wants to plant them in rows so that each row has the same number of plants and only one kind of plant. Find the least number of rows she needs.

Full solution

Given: 360 roses, 540 marigolds. Asked: the least number of rows.

Concept used: HCF (Topic 4). Why it applies: fewest rows means the largest equal row size, and the row size must divide both 360 and 540.

  1. 1

    Factorise.

    360=23×32×5,540=22×33×5360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5, \qquad 540 = 2^2 \times 3^3 \times 5360=23×32×5,540=22×33×5Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    HCF: smallest powers of 2, 3, 5.

    HCF=22×32×5=180\text{HCF} = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 180HCF=22×32×5=180Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    So each row has 180 plants. Number of rows.

    360180+540180=2+3=5\dfrac{360}{180} + \dfrac{540}{180} = 2 + 3 = 5180360​+180540​=2+3=5Swipe to see the whole equation →

  4. Check: 5×180=900=360+5405 \times 180 = 900 = 360 + 5405×180=900=360+540 ✔.

  5. Answer 5 rows5 \text{ rows}5 rows (2 of roses, 3 of marigolds), with 180 plants in each row.

    Common trap: Answering 180, or using the LCM (1 080) because the question says "least". "Least number of rows" is an HCF question; then count the rows.

P15●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Three athletes run round a track. They take 60 seconds, 72 seconds and 90 seconds per lap. They start together from the same point and run in the same direction. After how many minutes will all three be together at the starting point for the first time? How many laps will each have run by then?

Full solution

Given: lap times 60 s, 72 s, 90 s. Asked: the first time all three are at the start; laps for each.

Concept used: LCM (Topic 4). Why it applies: each athlete is at the start only at multiples of their lap time.

  1. 1

    Factorise.

    60=22×3×5,72=23×32,90=2×32×560 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5, \qquad 72 = 2^3 \times 3^2, \qquad 90 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 560=22×3×5,72=23×32,90=2×32×5Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    LCM: largest powers 232^323, 323^232, 5.

    LCM=23×32×5=360 s\text{LCM} = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360 \text{ s}LCM=23×32×5=360 sSwipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Convert to minutes.

    360 s=6 min360 \text{ s} = 6 \text{ min}360 s=6 minSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Laps: divide 360 by each lap time.

    36060=6,36072=5,36090=4\dfrac{360}{60} = 6, \qquad \dfrac{360}{72} = 5, \qquad \dfrac{360}{90} = 460360​=6,72360​=5,90360​=4Swipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: the lap counts are whole numbers ✔, and 360 s is more than every lap time ✔.

  6. Answer After 6 minutes6 \text{ minutes}6 minutes; the athletes run 6, 5 and 4 laps.

    Common trap: Giving "360" without units, or not converting to minutes as the question asks.

P16●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Find the smallest number which, when divided by 18, 27 and 45, leaves a remainder of 7 in each case.

Full solution

Given: divisors 18, 27, 45; remainder 7. Asked: the smallest such number.

Concept used: LCM + remainder (Topic 4). Why it applies: the number is 7 more than a common multiple of 18, 27 and 45.

  1. 1

    Factorise.

    18=2×32,27=33,45=32×518 = 2 \times 3^2, \qquad 27 = 3^3, \qquad 45 = 3^2 \times 518=2×32,27=33,45=32×5Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    LCM: largest powers 222, 333^333, 555.

    LCM=2×33×5=270\text{LCM} = 2 \times 3^3 \times 5 = 270LCM=2×33×5=270Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Add the remainder.

    270+7=277270 + 7 = 277270+7=277Swipe to see the whole equation →

  4. Check: 277=18×15+7=27×10+7=45×6+7277 = 18 \times 15 + 7 = 27 \times 10 + 7 = 45 \times 6 + 7277=18×15+7=27×10+7=45×6+7 ✔.

  5. Answer 277277277

    Common trap: Using the HCF (9) — the number must be bigger than all three divisors, so it comes from the LCM.

P17●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Show that 5×9×11+9×135 \times 9 \times 11 + 9 \times 135×9×11+9×13 is a composite number.

Full solution

Given: the expression. Asked: show it is composite.

Concept used: take out a common factor (Topic 2). Why it applies: 9 appears in both terms.

  1. 1

    Take out the common factor 9.

P18●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Check whether 22n22^n22n can end with the digit 0 or with the digit 5 for any natural number n.

Full solution

Given: 22n22^n22n. Asked: can it end in 0 or 5?

Concept used: prime factorisation of a power; uniqueness (Topic 2). Why it applies: ending in 0 needs 2 and 5; ending in 5 needs a factor 5 and an odd number.

  1. 1

    Factorise.

    22n=(2×11)n=2n×11n22^n = (2 \times 11)^n = 2^n \times 11^n22n=(2×11)n=2n×11nSwipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    By uniqueness, the only primes are 2 and 11 — there is no 5.

  3. 3

    Ending in 0 needs a factor 5 — not possible.

  4. 4

    Ending in 5 also needs a factor 5 (every number ending in 5 is divisible by 5) — not possible. (And 22n22^n22n is even, so it could not end in 5 anyway.)

  5. Check: 22,484,10 64822, 484, 10\,64822,484,10648 end in 2, 4, 8 ✔.

  6. Answer No — 22n22^n22n ends in neither 0 nor 5 for any natural number n.

P19●● StandardProof · 3 marksOriginal

Prove that 11\sqrt{11}11​ is irrational.

Full solution

Given: the theorem on primes and squares. To prove: 11\sqrt{11}11​ is irrational.

Concept used: seven-stage contradiction template (Topic 5). Why it applies: 11 is prime.

  1. 1

    Assume the opposite. Suppose 11\sqrt{11}11​ is rational: 11=ab\sqrt{11} = \dfrac{a}{b}11​=ba​, where a and b are integers, b≠0b \neq 0b=0, and a and b are co-prime.

  2. 2

    Multiply both sides by b.

    11 b=a\sqrt{11}\,b = a11​b=aSwipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Square both sides.

    11b2=a211b^2 = a^211b2=a2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    11 divides a2a^2a2 and 11 is prime, so 11 divides a. Write a=11ca = 11ca=11c.

  5. 5

    Substitute.

    11b2=121c211b^2 = 121c^211b2=121c2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Divide by 11.

    b2=11c2b^2 = 11c^2b2=11c2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    So 11 divides b2b^2b2, and therefore 11 divides b.

  8. 8

    Contradiction: 11 divides both a and b, but a and b are co-prime.

  9. 9

    Conclude: the assumption is false.

  10. Answer Hence 11\sqrt{11}11​ is irrational.

    Common trap: Stopping at step 4. You must also show that 11 divides b — only then do you have a contradiction.

Given that 3\sqrt{3}3​ is irrational, prove that 5−235 - 2\sqrt{3}5−23​ is irrational.

Full solution

Given: 3\sqrt{3}3​ is irrational. To prove: 5−235 - 2\sqrt{3}5−23​ is irrational.

Concept used: contradiction; isolate the root (Topic 6). Why it applies: rational − (non-zero rational × irrational).

  1. 1

    Assume the opposite. Suppose 5−23=ab5 - 2\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{a}{b}5−23​=ba​, where a and b are integers and b≠0b \neq 0b=0.

    Subtract 5 from both sides.

    −23=ab−5=a−5bb-2\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{a}{b} - 5 = \dfrac{a - 5b}{b}−23​=ba​−5=ba−5b​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Divide both sides by −2-2−2.

    3=5b−a2b\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{5b - a}{2b}3​=2b5b−a​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Reason. a and b are integers and 2b≠02b \neq 02b=0, so 5b−a2b\dfrac{5b - a}{2b}2b5b−a​ is rational. So 3\sqrt{3}3​ would be rational.

  5. 5

    Contradiction — 3\sqrt{3}3​ is irrational. So the assumption is false.

  6. Answer Hence 5−235 - 2\sqrt{3}5−23​ is irrational.

    Common trap: Losing the minus sign in step 3 and writing a−5b2b\dfrac{a - 5b}{2b}2ba−5b​. Dividing by −2-2−2 changes both signs.

P22●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Find the errors in the proof

Kabir wrote this proof that 4+34 + \sqrt{3}4+3​ is irrational:

Let 4+3=ab4 + \sqrt{3} = \dfrac{a}{b}4+3​=ba​, where a and b are integers, b≠0b \neq 0b=0.
Then 3=ab−4=a−4b\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{a}{b} - 4 = \dfrac{a - 4}{b}3​=ba​−4=ba−4​. …(line 2)
But 3=1.732…\sqrt{3} = 1.732\ldots3​=1.732…, which does not repeat, so 3\sqrt{3}3​ is irrational. …(line 3)
This is a contradiction. Hence 4+34 + \sqrt{3}4+3​ is irrational.

Find the two errors and write a correct proof (you may use the fact that 3\sqrt{3}3​ is irrational).

Full solution

Given: Kabir's proof. Asked: the errors and a correct proof.

Concept used: the isolate-the-root method (Topic 6). Why it applies: each line must follow correctly from the one before.

  1. 1

    The errors

    Line 2 (algebra): ab−4=a−4bb\dfrac{a}{b} - 4 = \dfrac{a - 4b}{b}ba​−4=ba−4b​, not a−4b\dfrac{a - 4}{b}ba−4​ — the 4 must be multiplied by b.

  2. 2

    Line 3 (reasoning): a decimal value is not a reason, and the key sentence is missing: he never says why the right side is rational, so there is nothing for "3\sqrt{3}3​ is irrational" to contradict.

  3. 3

    Correct proof

    Assume the opposite. Suppose 4+3=ab4 + \sqrt{3} = \dfrac{a}{b}4+3​=ba​, where a and b are integers and b≠0b \neq 0b=0.

  4. 4

    Subtract 4 from both sides.

    3=ab−4=a−4bb\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{a}{b} - 4 = \dfrac{a - 4b}{b}3​=ba​−4=ba−4b​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Reason. a and b are integers, so a−4bb\dfrac{a - 4b}{b}ba−4b​ is rational. So 3\sqrt{3}3​ would be rational.

  6. 6

    Contradiction — 3\sqrt{3}3​ is irrational. Hence the assumption is false, and 4+34 + \sqrt{3}4+3​ is irrational.

  7. Answer Errors: line 2 should read a−4bb\dfrac{a - 4b}{b}ba−4b​; line 3 must say "a−4bb\dfrac{a - 4b}{b}ba−4b​ is rational (a, b integers), so 3\sqrt{3}3​ would be rational — a contradiction", not argue from decimals. Corrected proof as above.

    Common trap: Spotting only the algebra slip. The missing "why it is rational" line is the bigger error — it carries a mark.

    So the numbers are (45, 315) and (135, 225).

Prove that 2+7\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{7}2​+7​ is irrational. (You may use the fact that 2\sqrt{2}2​ is irrational.)

Full solution

Given: 2\sqrt{2}2​ is irrational. To prove: 2+7\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{7}2​+7​ is irrational.

Concept used: contradiction; move one root across and square (Topic 6). Why it applies: squaring removes one root.

  1. 1

    Assume the opposite. Suppose 2+7=r\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{7} = r2​+7​=r, where r is rational (and r>0r > 0r>0).

  2. 2

    Subtract 2\sqrt{2}2​.

    7=r−2\sqrt{7} = r - \sqrt{2}7​=r−2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Square both sides.

    7=r2−2r2+27 = r^2 - 2r\sqrt{2} + 27=r2−2r2​+2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Rearrange.

    2r2=r2+2−7=r2−52r\sqrt{2} = r^2 + 2 - 7 = r^2 - 52r2​=r2+2−7=r2−5Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Divide by 2r2r2r (r>0r > 0r>0).

    2=r2−52r\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{r^2 - 5}{2r}2​=2rr2−5​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Reason. r is rational, so r2−52r\dfrac{r^2 - 5}{2r}2rr2−5​ is rational. So 2\sqrt{2}2​ would be rational.

  7. 7

    Contradiction — 2\sqrt{2}2​ is irrational. So the assumption is false.

  8. Answer Hence 2+7\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{7}2​+7​ is irrational.

    Common trap: (r−2)2=r2−2(r - \sqrt{2})^2 = r^2 - 2(r−2​)2=r2−2. The middle term −2r2-2r\sqrt{2}−2r2​ is the whole point of the method.

P27●●● AdvancedCase/source-based · 4 marksOriginal

Case: Sports day

On sports day, two drummers lead the march past. One drummer beats the big drum every 12 seconds, the other every 18 seconds; they start together. For the opening drill, 252 boys and 216 girls must stand in rows of equal size, each row having only boys or only girls, with as few rows as possible. In the relay event, three runners take 48 s, 60 s and 72 s for one lap.

(a) After how many seconds will the two drums next be beaten together? (1)
(b) How many students should stand in each row for the drill? (1)
(c) How many rows will there be in all? (2)

OR
(c) If the three runners start together, after how many minutes will they all be at the start together again, and how many laps will each have run? (2)

Full solution

Given: drum intervals 12 s and 18 s; 252 boys, 216 girls; lap times 48, 60, 72 s. Asked: parts (a)–(c).

Concept used: LCM for things that line up; HCF for the largest equal groups (Topic 4). Why it applies: (a) and (c OR) wait for cycles; (b) and (c) split into groups.

  1. 1

    (a)

    12=22×312 = 2^2 \times 312=22×3, 18=2×3218 = 2 \times 3^218=2×32; LCM =22×32=36= 2^2 \times 3^2 = 36=22×32=36. The drums are next beaten together after 36 s.

  2. 2

    (b)

    252=22×32×7252 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7252=22×32×7, 216=23×33216 = 2^3 \times 3^3216=23×33; HCF =22×32=36= 2^2 \times 3^2 = 36=22×32=36. Each row has 36 students.

  3. 3

    (c)

    Rows: 25236+21636=7+6=13\dfrac{252}{36} + \dfrac{216}{36} = 7 + 6 = 1336252​+36216​=7+6=13.

  4. 4

    (c) OR

    48=24×348 = 2^4 \times 348=24×3, 60=22×3×560 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 560=22×3×5, 72=23×3272 = 2^3 \times 3^272=23×32; LCM =24×32×5=720= 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 720=24×32×5=720 s =12= 12=12 min.

  5. 5

    Laps: 72048=15\dfrac{720}{48} = 1548720​=15, 72060=12\dfrac{720}{60} = 1260720​=12, 72072=10\dfrac{720}{72} = 1072720​=10.

  6. Check: 13×36=468=252+21613 \times 36 = 468 = 252 + 21613×36=468=252+216 ✔.

  7. Answer (a) 36 s (b) 36 students (c) 13 rows (c OR) 12 minutes; 15, 12 and 10 laps.

    Common trap: In (b), choosing the LCM because the drill is "bigger" — the row size must divide both 252 and 216.

P29●●● AdvancedTrue/False with justification · 3 marksOriginal

State whether each statement is true or false. Justify each answer.
(i) The sum of two irrational numbers is always irrational.
(ii) The product of a non-zero rational number and an irrational number is always irrational.
(iii) The quotient of two irrational numbers can be rational.

Full solution

Given: three statements. Asked: true/false with reasons.

Concept used: the rules need one rational number; a counter-example disproves "always" (Topic 6). Why it applies: each statement is a general claim.

  1. 1

    (i)

    False. 7−37 - \sqrt{3}7−3​ and 3\sqrt{3}3​ are both irrational, but (7−3)+3=7(7 - \sqrt{3}) + \sqrt{3} = 7(7−3​)+3​=7, rational.

  2. 2

    (ii)

    True. Suppose r≠0r \neq 0r=0 is rational, s is irrational and rs=trs = trs=t were rational. Then s=trs = \dfrac{t}{r}s=rt​, a rational divided by a non-zero rational — rational. Contradiction.

  3. 3

    (iii)

    True. 18\sqrt{18}18​ and 2\sqrt{2}2​ are irrational, but 182=9=3\dfrac{\sqrt{18}}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{9} = 32​18​​=9​=3, rational.

  4. Check: (iii) 18=32\sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}18​=32​, so 322=3\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 32​32​​=3 ✔.

  5. Answer (i) False (ii) True (iii) True — reasons as above.

    Common trap: In (ii), giving only one example ("232\sqrt{3}23​ is irrational"). One example cannot prove "always"; give the short argument.

P30●●● AdvancedProof · 3 marksOriginal

Prove that 6\sqrt{6}6​ is irrational.

Full solution

Given: the theorem on primes and squares. To prove: 6\sqrt{6}6​ is irrational.

Concept used: the contradiction template, using the prime 2 (6 itself is not prime). Why it applies: the theorem may be used only with a prime.

  1. 1

    Assume the opposite. Suppose 6=ab\sqrt{6} = \dfrac{a}{b}6​=ba​, where a and b are integers, b≠0b \neq 0b=0, and a and b are co-prime.

  2. 2

    Multiply by b and square.

    6b2=a26b^2 = a^26b2=a2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    a2=2×3b2a^2 = 2 \times 3b^2a2=2×3b2, so 2 divides a2a^2a2. Since 2 is prime, 2 divides a. Write a=2ca = 2ca=2c.

  4. 4

    Substitute.

    6b2=4c26b^2 = 4c^26b2=4c2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Divide by 2.

    3b2=2c23b^2 = 2c^23b2=2c2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    So 3b23b^23b2 is even. 3 is odd, so b2b^2b2 must be even (odd × odd is odd). So 2 divides b2b^2b2, and since 2 is prime, 2 divides b.

  7. 7

    Contradiction: 2 divides both a and b, but a and b are co-prime.

  8. 8

    Conclude: the assumption is false.

  9. Answer Hence 6\sqrt{6}6​ is irrational.

    Common trap: Writing "6 divides a2a^2a2, so 6 divides a" — the theorem is stated for primes only, and 6 is not prime. Work with the prime 2 (or 3) instead.

    Reasoning for each option: (A) ✘ uses y1y^1y1, but both numbers contain y2y^2y2. (B) ✔. (C) ✘ is the LCM. (D) ✘ uses x2x^2x2, but b has only x1x^1x1.

  3. Check: with x = 2, y = 3: a = 72, b = 54, HCF = 18 = 2×322 \times 3^22×32 ✔.

  4. Answer (B)

The product of a non-zero rational and an irrational number is

(non-zero rational) × irrational is irrational (Topic 6). Why it applies: if the product r × s were rational, then s = product ÷ r would be rational.

E6● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 1, Ex 1.2 Q6

The numbers 525 and 3000 are both divisible only by 3, 5, 15, 25 and 75. What is HCF (525, 3000)? Justify your answer.

Full solution

Given: the common divisors of 525 and 3000 (other than 1) are 3, 5, 15, 25, 75. Asked: the HCF, with a reason.

Concept used: the HCF is the highest common factor (Topic 3). Why it applies: we are told all the common factors.

  1. 1

    The largest of the common divisors 3, 5, 15, 25, 75 is 75.

  2. 2

    So HCF(525, 3000) = 75.

  3. Check: 525=3×52×7525 = 3 \times 5^2 \times 7525=3×52×7, 3000=23×3×533000 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5^33000=23×3×53, so HCF =3×52=75= 3 \times 5^2 = 75=3×52=75 ✔.

  4. Answer 757575 — it is the highest of the common factors.

E7● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 1, Ex 1.2 Q7

Explain why 3×5×7+73 \times 5 \times 7 + 73×5×7+7 is a composite number.

Full solution

Given: 3×5×7+73 \times 5 \times 7 + 73×5×7+7. Asked: why it is composite.

Concept used: take out a common factor (Topic 2).

  1. 1

    3×5×7+7=7×(3×5+1)=7×163 \times 5 \times 7 + 7 = 7 \times (3 \times 5 + 1) = 7 \times 163×5×7+7=7×(3×5+1)=7×16.

  2. 2

    It has the factor 7 (and 16), other than 1 and itself, so it is composite.

  3. Check: 105+7=112=7×16105 + 7 = 112 = 7 \times 16105+7=112=7×16 ✔.

  4. Answer =7×16=112= 7 \times 16 = 112=7×16=112, which has factors other than 1 and itself — composite.

E8●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 1, Ex 1.2 Q8

Can two numbers have 18 as their HCF and 380 as their LCM? Give reasons.

Full solution

Given: HCF 18, LCM 380. Asked: possible or not?

Concept used: the HCF always divides the LCM (Topic 3). Why it applies: check whether 18 divides 380.

  1. 1

    380÷18=21380 \div 18 = 21380÷18=21 remainder 2, so 18 does not divide 380.

  2. 2

    The HCF divides each number and each number divides the LCM, so the HCF must divide the LCM.

  3. Answer No — 18 does not divide 380, but the HCF of two numbers always divides their LCM.

E9●●● AdvancedProof · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 1, Ex 1.3 Q10

Prove that 3+5\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{5}3​+5​ is irrational.

Full solution

Given: 3\sqrt{3}3​ is irrational (Topic 5). To prove: 3+5\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{5}3​+5​ is irrational.

Concept used: contradiction; move one root and square (Topic 6).

  1. 1

    Assume the opposite. Suppose 3+5=r\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{5} = r3​+5​=r, r rational, r>0r > 0r>0.

  2. 2

    5=r−3\sqrt{5} = r - \sqrt{3}5​=r−3​.

  3. 3

    Square: 5=r2−2r3+35 = r^2 - 2r\sqrt{3} + 35=r2−2r3​+3.

  4. 4

    Rearrange: 2r3=r2−22r\sqrt{3} = r^2 - 22r3​=r2−2.

  5. 5

    Divide by 2r2r2r: 3=r2−22r\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{r^2 - 2}{2r}3​=2rr2−2​, which is rational since r is rational and r≠0r \neq 0r=0.

  6. 6

    Contradiction — 3\sqrt{3}3​ is irrational. Hence 3+5\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{5}3​+5​ is irrational.

  7. Answer Hence 3+5\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{5}3​+5​ is irrational.

E10●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 1, Ex 1.3 Q11

Show that 12n12^n12n cannot end with the digit 0 or 5 for any natural number n.

Full solution

Given: 12n12^n12n. Asked: show it never ends in 0 or 5.

Concept used: prime factorisation of a power; uniqueness (Topic 2).

  1. 1

    12n=(22×3)n=22n×3n12^n = (2^2 \times 3)^n = 2^{2n} \times 3^n12n=(22×3)n=22n×3n.

  2. 2

    By uniqueness, the only primes are 2 and 3. A number ending in 0 or 5 is divisible by 5, but 5 is not a factor of 12n12^n12n.

  3. Check: 12,144,1728,20 73612, 144, 1728, 20\,73612,144,1728,20736 end in 2, 4, 8, 6 ✔.

  4. Answer 12n=22n×3n12^n = 2^{2n} \times 3^n12n=22n×3n has no factor 5, so it never ends in 0 or 5.

E11●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 1, Ex 1.3 Q12

On a morning walk, three persons step off together and their steps measure 40 cm, 42 cm and 45 cm, respectively. What is the minimum distance each should walk so that each can cover the same distance in complete steps?

Full solution

Given: step lengths 40, 42, 45 cm. Asked: the minimum common distance in complete steps.

Concept used: LCM (Topic 4). Why it applies: the distance must be a whole number of steps for each person — a common multiple — and as small as possible.

  1. 1

    40=23×540 = 2^3 \times 540=23×5, 42=2×3×742 = 2 \times 3 \times 742=2×3×7, 45=32×545 = 3^2 \times 545=32×5.

  2. 2

    LCM =23×32×5×7=2520= 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 2520=23×32×5×7=2520.

  3. Check: 2520÷40=632520 \div 40 = 632520÷40=63, 2520÷42=602520 \div 42 = 602520÷42=60, 2520÷45=562520 \div 45 = 562520÷45=56 steps ✔.

  4. Answer 2520 cm2520 \text{ cm}2520 cm (25.2 m)

E12●●● AdvancedProof · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 1, Ex 1.3 Q14

Prove that p+q\sqrt{p} + \sqrt{q}p​+q​ is irrational, where p, q are primes.

Full solution

Given: p and q are primes, so p\sqrt{p}p​ is irrational (Topic 5). To prove: p+q\sqrt{p} + \sqrt{q}p​+q​ is irrational.

Concept used: contradiction; move one root and square (Topic 6).

  1. 1

    Assume the opposite. Suppose p+q=r\sqrt{p} + \sqrt{q} = rp​+q​=r, r rational, r>0r > 0r>0.

  2. 2

    q=r−p\sqrt{q} = r - \sqrt{p}q​=r−p​.

  3. 3

    Square: q=r2−2rp+pq = r^2 - 2r\sqrt{p} + pq=r2−2rp​+p.

  4. 4

    Rearrange: 2rp=r2+p−q2r\sqrt{p} = r^2 + p - q2rp​=r2+p−q.

  5. 5

    Divide by 2r2r2r: p=r2+p−q2r\sqrt{p} = \dfrac{r^2 + p - q}{2r}p​=2rr2+p−q​, which is rational (r, p, q rational, r≠0r \neq 0r=0).

  6. 6

    Contradiction — p\sqrt{p}p​ is irrational because p is prime. Hence p+q\sqrt{p} + \sqrt{q}p​+q​ is irrational.

  7. Answer Hence p+q\sqrt{p} + \sqrt{q}p​+q​ is irrational. (The argument also covers p = q, when the sum is 2p2\sqrt{p}2p​.)

C1 — Case: the class library● FoundationCase/source-based · 5 marksCBSE Mathematics Class X Case Study Question Bank, Real Numbers, Case Study 1

To enhance the reading skills of grade X students, the school nominates you and two of your friends to set up a class library. There are two sections — section A and section B of grade X. There are 32 students in section A and 36 students in section B.

  1. What is the minimum number of books you will acquire for the class library, so that they can be distributed equally among students of Section A or Section B? (a) 144 (b) 128 (c) 288 (d) 272
  2. If the product of two positive integers is equal to the product of their HCF and LCM is true then, the HCF (32, 36) is (a) 2 (b) 4 (c) 6 (d) 8
  3. 36 can be expressed as a product of its primes as (a) 22×322^2 \times 3^222×32 (b) 21×332^1 \times 3^321×33 (c) 23×312^3 \times 3^123×31 (d) 20×302^0 \times 3^020×30
  4. 7×11×13×15+157 \times 11 \times 13 \times 15 + 157×11×13×15+15 is a (a) Prime number (b) Composite number (c) Neither prime nor composite (d) None of the above
  5. If p and q are positive integers such that p=ab2p = ab^2p=ab2 and q=a2bq = a^2bq=a2b, where a, b are prime numbers, then the LCM (p, q) is (a) ababab (b) a2b2a^2b^2a2b2 (c) a3b2a^3b^2a3b2 (d) a3b3a^3b^3a3b3

Full solution

Given: 32 and 36 students, and four related questions. Asked: five answers.

Concept used: LCM for "shared equally among A or B" (a common multiple), HCF, prime factorisation, common factor, LCM from powers (Topics 2–4).

  1. 1

    The number of books must be a multiple of 32 and of 36: 32=2532 = 2^532=25, 36=22×3236 = 2^2 \times 3^236=22×32, LCM =25×32=288= 2^5 \times 3^2 = 288=25×32=288 → (c).

  2. 2

    HCF =22=4= 2^2 = 4=22=4 → (b). (Check: 4×288=1152=32×364 \times 288 = 1152 = 32 \times 364×288=1152=32×36.)

  3. 3

    36=22×3236 = 2^2 \times 3^236=22×32 → (a).

  4. 4

    15×(7×11×13+1)=15×100215 \times (7 \times 11 \times 13 + 1) = 15 \times 100215×(7×11×13+1)=15×1002 — composite → (b).

  5. 5

    Largest powers: a2a^2a2, b2b^2b2 → LCM =a2b2= a^2b^2=a2b2 → (b).

  6. Answer 1 (c) · 2 (b) · 3 (a) · 4 (b) · 5 (b)

    Common trap: In part 1, choosing 144 or 128 (4×364 \times 364×36, 4×324 \times 324×32: the HCF times one class size). "Distributed equally among A or B" means the total must suit both class sizes — a common multiple.

C2 — Case: the seminar rooms●● StandardCase/source-based · 5 marksCBSE Mathematics Class X Case Study Question Bank, Real Numbers, Case Study 2

A seminar is being conducted by an Educational Organisation, where the participants will be educators of different subjects. The number of participants in Hindi, English and Mathematics are 60, 84 and 108 respectively.

  1. In each room the same number of participants are to be seated and all of them being in the same subject, hence maximum number participants that can accommodated in each room are (a) 14 (b) 12 (c) 16 (d) 18
  2. What is the minimum number of rooms required during the event? (a) 11 (b) 31 (c) 41 (d) 21
  3. The LCM of 60, 84 and 108 is (a) 3780 (b) 3680 (c) 4780 (d) 4680
  4. The product of HCF and LCM of 60, 84 and 108 is (a) 55360 (b) 35360 (c) 45500 (d) 45360
  5. 108 can be expressed as a product of its primes as (a) 23×322^3 \times 3^223×32 (b) 23×332^3 \times 3^323×33 (c) 22×322^2 \times 3^222×32 (d) 22×332^2 \times 3^322×33

Full solution

Given: 60, 84, 108 participants. Asked: five answers.

Concept used: HCF for equal groups and fewest rooms; LCM by the table (Topics 3 and 4).

  1. 1

    60=22×3×560 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 560=22×3×5, 84=22×3×784 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 784=22×3×7, 108=22×33108 = 2^2 \times 3^3108=22×33. HCF =22×3=12= 2^2 \times 3 = 12=22×3=12 → (b).

  2. 2

    Rooms =6012+8412+10812=5+7+9=21= \dfrac{60}{12} + \dfrac{84}{12} + \dfrac{108}{12} = 5 + 7 + 9 = 21=1260​+1284​+12108​=5+7+9=21 → (d).

  3. 3

    LCM =22×33×5×7=3780= 2^2 \times 3^3 \times 5 \times 7 = 3780=22×33×5×7=3780 → (a).

  4. 4

    HCF × LCM =12×3780=45 360= 12 \times 3780 = 45\,360=12×3780=45360 → (d). Notice this is not 60×84×108=544 32060 \times 84 \times 108 = 544\,32060×84×108=544320 — the product rule fails for three numbers.

  5. 5

    108=22×33108 = 2^2 \times 3^3108=22×33 → (d).

  6. Answer 1 (b) · 2 (d) · 3 (a) · 4 (d) · 5 (d)

    Common trap: Part 2 says "minimum", which tempts students towards the LCM. Fewest rooms means the largest group per room — the HCF — and then you add up the rooms.

A Mathematics Exhibition is being conducted in your School and one of your friends is making a model of a factor tree. He has some difficulty and asks for your help in completing a quiz for the audience. Observe the following factor tree and answer the following:
(Factor tree described in words: x splits into 5 and 2783; 2783 splits into y and 253; 253 splits into 11 and z.)

  1. What will be the value of x? (a) 15005 (b) 13915 (c) 56920 (d) 17429
  2. What will be the value of y? (a) 23 (b) 22 (c) 11 (d) 19
  3. What will be the value of z? (a) 22 (b) 23 (c) 17 (d) 19
  4. According to Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic 13915 is a (a) Composite number (b) Prime number (c) Neither prime nor composite (d) Even number
  5. The prime factorisation of 13915 is (a) 5×113×1325 \times 11^3 \times 13^25×113×132 (b) 5×113×2325 \times 11^3 \times 23^25×113×232 (c) 5×112×235 \times 11^2 \times 235×112×23 (d) 5×112×1325 \times 11^2 \times 13^25×112×132

Full solution

Given: the factor tree. Asked: x, y, z and the factorisation.

Concept used: each node is the product of its two branches (Topic 2).

  1. 1

    x=5×2783=13 915x = 5 \times 2783 = 13\,915x=5×2783=13915 → (b).

  2. 2

    2783=y×2532783 = y \times 2532783=y×253, so y=2783÷253=11y = 2783 \div 253 = 11y=2783÷253=11 → (c).

    253=11×z253 = 11 \times z253=11×z, so z=23z = 23z=23 → (b).

    13 915 has factors other than 1 and itself → composite → (a).

    Leaves: 5, 11, 11, 23 → 5×112×235 \times 11^2 \times 235×112×23 → (c).

  6. Answer 1 (b) · 2 (c) · 3 (b) · 4 (a) · 5 (c)
